claims.text: The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy has severe atomic-scale lattice distortions arising from heterogeneous atomic radii.
Elastic-modulus mismatch among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr contributes to lattice distortion in the alloy.
Lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr generate localized stress fields.
The localized stress fields intrinsically impede dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation motion produces greater dislocation pinning in WTaTiVZr.
Impeded dislocation motion produces a higher dislocation density in WTaTiVZr.
Dislocation barriers and pinning enhance work hardening in WTaTiVZr at high temperature.
The lattice-distortion-mediated dislocation behavior enhances dynamic recovery at high temperature.
The proposed dislocation behavior increases plastic strain before failure in WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
The proposed dislocation behavior improves the toughness of WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
Under otherwise identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher dislocation density than pure tungsten.
Under otherwise identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit more persistent and pinned dislocation configurations than pure tungsten.
Under otherwise identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher work-hardening rate than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a more homogeneous lattice and therefore fewer intrinsic barriers to dislocation movement than WTaTiVZr.
Pure tungsten consequently has lower high-temperature work hardening, plasticity, and toughness than WTaTiVZr.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies from 800 to 1000 °C under plasma-facing-component-relevant loading.
At lower temperatures, other deformation mechanisms may dominate over the proposed lattice-distortion mechanism.
Grain-boundary effects or other microstructural variations may become significant enough to obscure the proposed mechanism.
Matching starting microstructures and loading conditions will reduce, but not necessarily eliminate, extraneous differences between the alloy and pure tungsten.
Limited sampled volume may restrict the statistical robustness of in-situ TEM observations.
